newsitem.title: FRANCE: First novel about kamikaze flier wins Goncourt prize.
newsitem.headline: First novel about kamikaze flier wins Goncourt prize.

text.p: A first-time novelist's story about a woman probing the death of her father at the hands of a Japanese suicide pilot won France's top literary award on Tuesday.
Pascale Roze won the Goncourt prize for her novel "Le Chasseur Zero" (Fighter Plane Zero). Nominally worth 50 francs ($10), it usually secures high sales for the winning novel.
The prize is given annually at a gourmet lunch in Paris by 10 literary personalities. It was only the fourth time that a debut novelist has taken the award.
The book won the prize at the third ballot, juror Dider Decoin said in a statement carried live by French television.

The ballot split the jury with five votes for and five against "Rhapsodie Cubaine" (Cuban Rhapsody) by Cuban-born French national Eduardo Manet. The president's vote counted double and ensured the prize went to Roze.
"I'm a bit stunned, I really didn't expect it," Roze, the eighth woman to win the prize, told France-2 television a few minutes after the announcement.

"The book is about a little girl whose father is killed by a kamikaze pilot in the Pacific War. The only way for her to reach her father is to die by getting close to the kamikaze. He is present inside her in the form of a buzzing in her ears, like a wasp," Roze said.
"When you fail to tell something to people, especially to a child, that thing can re-emerge in a totally unexpected and often monstrous way," she said.
The Goncourt prize was founded in 1903. Last year's winner, "Le Testament Francais" (The French Will) by Russian-born writer Andrei Makine has sold 520,000 copies.

Cautioned that Goncourt awards had in the past caused permanent writer's bloc in some winners, Roze answered: "I'm lucky because I have already started a second book. I'll try to be firm. The prize will allow me to take the time to finish this book."
She said that she had previously worked as an actress and planned to continue holding writers' workshops.

Literary pundits had tipped Manet and Canadian Nancy Huston as favourites but the newspaper Le Parisien reported that the jurors planned to ensure the Goncourt for novels written in French went to a French-born writer.

In Roze's book, the girl is brought back to France by her widowed mother, a Frenchwoman, and is brought up by her austere grandparents. She discovers the truth about her father's death through a classmate.
Instead of searching for her father, the girl searches for his murderer and the kamikaze pilot eventually invades her life.

Another major literary award, the Renaudot prize, went to Boris Schreiber for "Un silence d'environ une demi-heure" (A Silence About Half-an-hour Long), a tale of a Jewish family's flight from Russia in the 1930s and 1940s.

The literary season kicked off last week when the Femina prize was awarded to French writer Genevieve Brisac for "Un Weekend de Chasse a la Mere" (A Weekend Hunting Mother), the tragic tale of a single mother fighting for custody of her son.
